notes: Fairbrother ranks every soul in the house by how long he has brushed their coats, trusts the Major least and the nephew most without saying either, and regards the new housekeeper as a question the master asked over his head and did not live to answer.

says.text: 'The Major has had the blue room eleven Christmases and takes his own boots off outside the door, which a gentleman does not. His own man never comes with him.' He pauses. 'He knows this house as well as the family, and better than some.'
'The Major is a guest of the house. Fairbrother treats him as one and would counsel the housekeeper to do the same, while she is housekeeper.'
'Major Carrington has had the blue room eleven Christmases. He rings for shaving water at seven and does not ring again. Fairbrother is asked nothing further and says nothing further.'

'Fairbrother has cleaned Mr. Nathaniel's boots since he was in short coats. He has never once said thank you and never once needed telling where a thing was kept. He is not a running sort of young gentleman, whatever the yard saw on Thursday.'

'Dr. Ashcombe dines twice a quarter and sat up three nights in March when the master's chest was bad. He drinks the master's port as though he expects to be paid in it. Fairbrother decants it all the same.'

'Miss Gresham rings for hot water at seven and again at the half hour, and is dressed before either can arrive. Fairbrother does not know what a young lady does with a half hour she has already used. He only carries the cans.'

'Miss Evangeline has the run of the library and the old dog and the master's temper when she wanted it. She was the one person under this roof he did not raise his voice to.' He straightens a glove on the tray. 'Fairbrother does not say that lightly.'
'Mrs. Ormsby takes the yellow room for her knees, it being nearest the stairs. Her knees managed the gallery quick enough when the poker was called for. She was at the door before the doctor.'

'Netherby does the first-floor grates and does them properly, and has been crying into the ash since Thursday. She was on the back stairs later than a housemaid should be.' He stops there. 'Fairbrother does not ask maids why they cry. That is the housekeeper's province now, and he would sooner it were asked kindly.'
'Netherby does the first-floor grates and does them properly, and has been crying into the ash since Thursday. Fairbrother does not ask maids why they cry. That is the housekeeper's province now.'

'Mr. Ellingham came up on the Tuesday with a bag he has not let out of his sight and sleeps with his boots by the bed as if he means to leave in them. He has twice asked Fairbrother whether the master's desk locks.' A slow breath. 'It does.'

'Quarles has kept the lodge thirty years and has never once come up to the house without being sent for. This morning he walked four feet of snow to the kitchen door without being sent for. Fairbrother gave him tea and did not ask.'

'Eleven doors and the master's at the end of it. Fairbrother has walked that gallery with a candle more nights than the housekeeper has been alive. The boards speak outside the Major's door and go quiet outside the widow's; one learns where to put one's feet.'

'The back stairs are for the household and the coals, and for such guests as do not care to be met on the front. The lamp there is not lit after ten. Anyone wanting to go up after ten takes a candle from the shelf, and the shelf has tallow, not wax.'

'Fairbrother has drawn out the master's chair at the head of that table every evening for twenty years. On Thursday no one had told him not to, and he drew it out, and it sat there empty through five courses with the Major talking across it.'

'Mrs. Pell had that room twenty-two years. Her chair is still turned to the fire the way she liked it, and the key of the store cupboard still hangs on the second hook, not the first.' He does not look at you. 'Fairbrother would be obliged if both were left so.'
'The hall takes its tone from the top of the table. It has been very quiet at the top of the table these two days, and the boy has stopped whistling. Fairbrother is aware of it.'

'The drawing-room fire is kept up for the ladies. The Major has taken the chair nearest it, which was the master's chair, and has not been told so. Fairbrother did not consider it his place to tell him.'

'Fairbrother laid the study fire and two white wax candles at six every evening for forty years. White wax from the chandler at Lichfield. The master would not have tallow in that room; the smell got into the books.'

'Dr. Ashcombe asked whether the ice house would take a man. Fairbrother told him it would take a side of beef, and the doctor took that for his answer. The path to it has not been cleared, and Fairbrother has not been asked to clear it.'

'The library shares a chimney with the study. On a still night a person in the one can hear a chair pushed back in the other.' He considers the window. 'Thursday was not a still night. Miss Evangeline was in there until the candles went, as she always is.'

'The Major called for the poker before anyone had tried the handle twice. Fairbrother heard the key go down on the carpet inside before the wood gave. He has been asked since whether he is sure of that. He has dropped enough keys on enough carpets to know the sound.'

'Fairbrother served the soup and heard the word magistrate before the fish. Mr. Nathaniel went out by the service door, which he has not used since he was a boy stealing jam. Fairbrother had him by the collar in the yard, and was told to sit at his door, and sat.'

'The Major sent Netherby up with a scuttle to a dead man's grate. Fairbrother went up behind her and stood in the study doorway until she had finished, so that nothing went into her pail that was not ash. He then came down to be sent for.'

'The blue-room door drops on its hinges in wet weather and must be lifted to shut quietly, or it bangs. It did not bang on Thursday night. The Major has stayed eleven Christmases; he knows how to lift it.'

'Oak, with the lock put in new in 'sixty-one and the one key on the master's chain. Fairbrother has oiled it every Lady Day since. It would not have wanted a poker had anyone sent for the carpenter, but the Major did not care to wait.'

'The candle boxes sit on the shelf by the back-stairs door, wax to the left and tallow to the right, as they have since Mrs. Pell's time. A person in the dark puts out a hand and knows which is which by the place. Fairbrother asks that nothing on that shelf be moved.'

'He was in it square to the desk, as he sat every night of his life, with his pen laid along the blotter. A man who has had a fright does not die tidy.' He says it to the carpet. 'Fairbrother has said that to the housekeeper and to no one else.'
'Fairbrother set the housekeeper's box square this morning. It was no liberty; it was standing in front of the tallow, and he has reached past it in the dark forty years.'
'Fairbrother has not touched the housekeeper's box. Should it be found short, she may count it aloud before the maids, as she counts other people's.'
'The housekeeper's box is the housekeeper's business. Fairbrother observes only that it has been put at the wrong end of the shelf.'

'The Major's greatcoat was on the stand at breakfast with the shoulders dry, after a night it snowed sideways on the yard. Fairbrother brushed it as he brushes it every morning. It is the Major's coat.'

'The boy sits the hall chair for the bell until the house goes up. On Thursday the boy was abed with his chest by ten and the chair stood empty. After ten, anyone crossing the hall crossed it unseen. The back stairs are another matter.'

'It is the one window on the back stairs and it gives on the yard. The snow light through it is enough to find a tread by and not enough to know a face. Fairbrother has gone up by it without a candle at all when the box was low.'

'Mrs. Ormsby keeps her door on the latch and her maid in the dressing room beyond it, only her maid did not come this year. She asked Fairbrother for the key of it the first night of the snow. She has turned it every night since.'

'Four, north-facing, with the frost on the inside since Tuesday; the master would not have the gallery fire lit for guests who were abed. From the third one can see the lodge lamp. The Major stood at the third a long while after the ladies went up on Thursday.'

'The press is on the first-floor landing and the housekeeper has the key of it now. There is a pillowslip gone from the second shelf since Thursday. Fairbrother counts linen as he counts candles; he does not say why a thing is gone, only that it is.'

'A cloth came back to the scullery on Friday morning with tallow on it and no one to say whose it was. Netherby had it in the copper before Fairbrother had looked at it twice.' He folds his hands. 'He has not asked her why. That is not his department.'
